units.title: Interpreting the Constitution
units.blurb: The kinds of argument used in constitutional cases, originalism and living constitutionalism presented as their advocates present them, and precedent in constitutional law.

units.title: The Judicial Power
units.blurb: Marbury and judicial review, review of state courts and judicial supremacy, Congress's control of jurisdiction, standing in constitutional cases and political questions.

units.title: Enumerated Powers and McCulloch
units.blurb: Congress as a government of enumerated powers, McCulloch v. Maryland and the Necessary and Proper Clause today.

units.title: The Commerce Power
units.blurb: From Gibbons v. Ogden through the narrow readings of 1887 to 1936, the turn of 1937, Wickard, the civil rights cases, Lopez and Morrison, Raich and NFIB.

units.title: Taxing and Spending
units.blurb: The taxing power, the spending power and the general welfare, conditions on federal grants, and the rule against commandeering the states.

units.title: Federalism and State Sovereignty
units.blurb: The Tenth Amendment as a limit, state sovereign immunity, Congress's power to enforce the Civil War amendments, and preemption.

units.title: The Dormant Commerce Clause and State Power
units.blurb: Limits on states that discriminate against or burden interstate commerce, the market participant exception and the Privileges and Immunities Clause of Article IV.

units.title: Separation of Powers
units.blurb: Youngstown and presidential power, nondelegation and major questions, the legislative veto and the line-item veto, appointments and removal, foreign affairs, war and detention, and executive privilege and immunity.

units.title: The Levels of Scrutiny
units.blurb: The framework courts use to review laws: rational basis, intermediate scrutiny and strict scrutiny, and how a court chooses among them. It carries over into Constitutional Law II.

topics.title: Kinds of Constitutional Argument
topics.short: Constitutional arguments draw on text, history (original understanding), structure (relations among institutions), precedent (doctrine), consequences (prudence) and national values (ethos); Philip Bobbitt called these the modalities of constitutional argument.
topics.trouble: Students label any argument they find weak as "policy." Each modality is a recognized form of argument; identify which one an opinion uses before judging it.

topics.title: Originalism
topics.short: Originalists hold that the Constitution's meaning was fixed when each provision was adopted, today usually as its original public meaning; advocates say this keeps judges bound by law rather than preference and leaves change to the amendment process.
topics.trouble: Students equate originalism with the framers' private intentions. Most originalists today look to the public meaning of the words when ratified, not what particular framers hoped.

topics.title: Living Constitutionalism
topics.short: Living constitutionalists hold that the Constitution's broad principles are applied to new conditions over time, often through precedent built case by case; advocates say this is how the common law and the Constitution have in fact developed and keeps it workable.
topics.trouble: Students think living constitutionalists ignore the text. They accept the text's authority; they read its open-ended phrases (such as "equal protection") as stating principles whose application can change.

topics.title: Precedent in Constitutional Cases
topics.short: Stare decisis is weaker in constitutional cases because only an amendment or the Court can correct an error; the Court weighs the quality of the reasoning, workability, consistency with related decisions, changed facts and reliance before overruling.
topics.trouble: Students think the Court rarely overrules itself. It has overruled its own precedents well over a hundred times, including Plessy (by Brown) and Lochner-era cases.

topics.title: Marbury v. Madison
topics.short: In Marbury v. Madison (1803) Chief Justice Marshall held that Marbury had a right to his commission and a legal remedy, but that the Court could not issue a writ of mandamus in its original jurisdiction because that part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional; courts must not enforce laws contrary to the Constitution.
topics.trouble: Students think Marbury held the Court is the only interpreter of the Constitution. Its holding is narrower: in deciding a case, a court must apply the Constitution over a conflicting statute.

topics.title: Review of State Courts and Judicial Supremacy
topics.short: Martin v. Hunter's Lessee (1816) upheld Supreme Court review of state court rulings on federal law; Cooper v. Aaron (1958), unanimous, held that state officials are bound by the Court's interpretation of the Constitution in Brown.
topics.trouble: Students think a state supreme court has the last word on federal questions. On federal law the U.S. Supreme Court can review it; on purely state law the state's highest court is final.

topics.title: Congress and the Courts' Jurisdiction
topics.short: Article III lets Congress make "Exceptions" to the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction and create (or not create) lower courts; in Ex parte McCardle (1869) the Court accepted Congress's repeal of its jurisdiction over a pending appeal; how far this power goes is debated.
topics.trouble: Students think Congress cannot touch the Court's jurisdiction. The Exceptions Clause gives Congress real power; scholars debate its outer limits, such as removing all courts from hearing a constitutional claim.

topics.title: Standing in Constitutional Cases
topics.short: Standing applies to constitutional claims too: taxpayers generally lack standing to challenge federal spending (Frothingham, 1923), with a narrow Establishment Clause exception (Flast v. Cohen, 1968) that Hein (2007) limited to congressional appropriations.
topics.trouble: Students think being a taxpayer gives standing to challenge any spending. The general rule is no; Flast's exception is narrow.

topics.title: The Political Question Doctrine
topics.short: Baker v. Carr (1962) held malapportionment claims justiciable and listed six markers of a political question; Nixon v. United States (1993) left Senate impeachment trial procedures to the Senate; Rucho v. Common Cause (2019) held partisan gerrymandering claims beyond federal courts.
topics.trouble: Students think Baker v. Carr refused to decide the case. Baker held that the apportionment claim was justiciable; its list of political-question factors is used to explain when courts should decline.

topics.title: A Government of Enumerated Powers
topics.short: Congress has only the powers the Constitution grants; most are in Article I, Section 8, and others in amendments' enforcement clauses; the Tenth Amendment confirms that other powers are reserved to the states or the people, and there is no general federal police power.
topics.trouble: Students think the General Welfare Clause gives Congress power to do anything for the general welfare. It is a power to tax and spend for the general welfare, not a general power to regulate.

topics.title: McCulloch v. Maryland
topics.short: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) the Court unanimously upheld the Second Bank of the United States as a means "plainly adapted" to Congress's enumerated ends and held that Maryland could not tax it, since "the power to tax involves the power to destroy."
topics.trouble: Students think McCulloch says Congress can do whatever is useful. The end must be legitimate and within an enumerated power; the clause concerns means. "Let the end be legitimate, let it be within the scope of the constitution…"

topics.title: Necessary and Proper Today
topics.short: United States v. Comstock (2010) upheld civil commitment of dangerous federal prisoners as a rational means connected to enumerated powers; in NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) Chief Justice Roberts wrote that the individual mandate was not a "proper" means under the clause.
topics.trouble: Students treat Comstock and NFIB as contradictory. Both accept McCulloch; they differ on whether a measure is a reasonable means that respects the structure of limited powers.

topics.title: Gibbons v. Ogden
topics.short: In Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) Marshall read "commerce" to include navigation and all commercial intercourse, and "among the several States" to reach commerce that concerns more states than one, so a federal coasting license overrode New York's steamboat monopoly.
topics.trouble: Students think Gibbons let Congress regulate everything. It defined commerce broadly but left purely internal commerce of a state to the state.

topics.title: The Narrow Era (1887 to 1936)
topics.short: The Court separated manufacturing from commerce (United States v. E. C. Knight, 1895), struck down a federal ban on goods made by child labor (Hammer v. Dagenhart, 1918) and struck down New Deal codes and coal regulation (Schechter Poultry, 1935; Carter Coal, 1936), using a direct-indirect effects test.
topics.trouble: Students think the Court struck down every economic law of the era. It upheld railroad rate regulation and many laws regulating goods moving across state lines (e.g., the lottery case, Champion v. Ames, 1903).

topics.title: The Turn of 1937
topics.short: NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel (1937) upheld the Wagner Act's reach to a steel company whose labor disputes affected interstate commerce; United States v. Darby (1941) upheld federal wage and hour rules and overruled Hammer v. Dagenhart.
topics.trouble: Students credit the change entirely to the court-packing plan. Jones & Laughlin was decided while the plan was pending, and historians debate how much the plan mattered; new appointments soon followed.

topics.title: Wickard v. Filburn
topics.short: In Wickard v. Filburn (1942) the Court upheld limits on wheat a farmer grew for use on his own farm, because the total (aggregate) effect of many farmers doing the same would substantially affect interstate commerce.
topics.trouble: Students think Filburn sold his extra wheat across state lines. He used it on his farm; the aggregation principle, not any sale, brought it within the commerce power.

topics.title: The Commerce Power and Civil Rights
topics.short: Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States and Katzenbach v. McClung (both 1964) upheld the Civil Rights Act of 1964's ban on discrimination in public accommodations as regulation of interstate commerce, through interstate travelers and food shipped across state lines.
topics.trouble: Students think the 1964 Act rested on the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court upheld its public accommodations provisions under the Commerce Clause, partly because the Civil Rights Cases (1883) had limited Congress's Fourteenth Amendment power over private businesses.

topics.title: United States v. Lopez
topics.short: In United States v. Lopez (1995), 5 to 4, the Court struck down the Gun-Free School Zones Act and named three categories Congress may regulate: the channels of interstate commerce, its instrumentalities and persons or things in it, and activities that substantially affect it; possessing a gun near a school was not economic activity.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the three Lopez categories. Channels are highways and waterways; instrumentalities are the vehicles and things moving; the third category is activities with substantial effects.

topics.title: United States v. Morrison
topics.short: In United States v. Morrison (2000), 5 to 4, the Court struck down the civil remedy in the Violence Against Women Act, holding that gender-motivated violence is not economic activity and that its effects could not be aggregated, and that Section 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment does not reach private conduct.
topics.trouble: Students think Morrison struck down the whole Violence Against Women Act. Only the civil-remedy provision was at issue.

topics.title: Gonzales v. Raich
topics.short: In Gonzales v. Raich (2005), 6 to 3, the Court upheld applying the federal Controlled Substances Act to marijuana grown at home for medical use under California law, relying on Wickard because the activity was part of a broader economic market Congress could regulate.
topics.trouble: Students think Raich overruled Lopez. The Court distinguished Lopez: Raich involved economic activity (producing a commodity) within a comprehensive regulatory scheme.

topics.title: NFIB v. Sebelius: Commerce
topics.short: In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) five justices concluded the Commerce Clause did not support the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate, because it compelled people to enter commerce rather than regulating existing activity; the mandate was upheld as a tax.
topics.trouble: Students think NFIB struck down the mandate. It held the commerce argument failed but upheld the mandate under the taxing power, 5 to 4.

topics.title: The Taxing Power
topics.short: Congress may tax to raise revenue even if the tax also discourages conduct, but a "tax" that is really a penalty may fail (Bailey v. Drexel Furniture, 1922); NFIB (2012) upheld the mandate's payment as a tax because it was modest, not tied to willfulness and collected by the IRS.
topics.trouble: Students think the label Congress uses decides whether something is a tax. Courts look at function, not label: NFIB treated a "penalty" as a tax for constitutional purposes.

topics.title: The Spending Power
topics.short: Congress may spend for the general welfare, a power not limited to the other enumerated subjects (United States v. Butler, 1936, adopting Hamilton's view over Madison's); Helvering v. Davis (1937) upheld Social Security's old-age benefits.
topics.trouble: Students think Butler upheld the farm program it reviewed. Butler accepted the broad Hamiltonian view of spending but struck down the Agricultural Adjustment Act on Tenth Amendment grounds.

topics.title: Conditions on Federal Money
topics.short: South Dakota v. Dole (1987) upheld withholding 5 percent of highway funds from states with a drinking age under 21, requiring conditions to be for the general welfare, unambiguous, related to the program and not otherwise unconstitutional, and not coercive; NFIB (2012) held the Medicaid expansion's threat to all existing Medicaid funds coercive.
topics.trouble: Students think Congress can attach any condition to any money. Dole's limits apply, and NFIB found coercion when the threatened loss was a large share of a state's budget.

topics.title: Anti-Commandeering
topics.short: Congress may not compel state legislatures to enact federal programs (New York v. United States, 1992) or order state officers to carry them out (Printz v. United States, 1997), and may not order states to keep their own laws on the books (Murphy v. NCAA, 2018).
topics.trouble: Students confuse commandeering with preemption. Congress may preempt state law or offer money with conditions; it may not issue direct orders to state governments to regulate.

topics.title: The Tenth Amendment as a Limit
topics.short: National League of Cities v. Usery (1976) barred federal wage rules for state employees in "traditional governmental functions"; Garcia v. San Antonio Metropolitan Transit Authority (1985) overruled it, leaving states' protection mostly to the political process.
topics.trouble: Students think the Tenth Amendment by itself lists powers that belong to the states. It reserves powers not delegated; which powers those are depends on the scope of the grants to Congress.

topics.title: State Sovereign Immunity
topics.short: Chisholm v. Georgia (1793) let a citizen of another state sue Georgia, and the Eleventh Amendment (1795) reversed it; Hans v. Louisiana (1890) barred suits by a state's own citizens; Seminole Tribe (1996) held Congress cannot abrogate immunity under Article I; Ex parte Young (1908) allows suits against state officers for injunctions.
topics.trouble: Students read the Eleventh Amendment literally, as covering only suits by citizens of other states. The Court treats it as confirming a broader immunity, though some justices and scholars disagree.

topics.title: Enforcing the Civil War Amendments
topics.short: Congress may enforce the Fourteenth Amendment by "appropriate legislation"; City of Boerne v. Flores (1997) requires "congruence and proportionality" between the injury and the remedy; Shelby County v. Holder (2013) struck down the Voting Rights Act's coverage formula as based on old data.
topics.trouble: Students think Shelby County struck down the whole Voting Rights Act. It struck the coverage formula of Section 4(b); Section 2's nationwide ban remains.

topics.title: Preemption
topics.short: Valid federal law preempts state law expressly (by its terms) or impliedly, when federal law occupies a field or conflicts with state law (it is impossible to obey both, or state law obstructs federal purposes); there is a presumption against preempting traditional state powers.
topics.trouble: Students think any overlap between federal and state law means preemption. Many state laws coexist with federal ones; preemption needs express words, a field, or a real conflict.

topics.title: Discrimination Against Interstate Commerce
topics.short: The Court reads the Commerce Clause to limit states even when Congress is silent: a state law that discriminates against out-of-state commerce is virtually per se invalid unless no other means can serve a legitimate local purpose (City of Philadelphia v. New Jersey, 1978; Maine v. Taylor, 1986).
topics.trouble: Students look for discrimination only in a law's words. Laws neutral on their face can discriminate in purpose or effect; on the other hand, some justices reject the doctrine entirely as lacking a textual basis.

topics.title: Pike Balancing
topics.short: A nondiscriminatory state law is upheld unless the burden on interstate commerce is "clearly excessive in relation to the putative local benefits" (Pike v. Bruce Church, 1970); Kassel v. Consolidated Freightways (1981) struck down Iowa's ban on long double-trailer trucks because its slight safety gain did not justify a heavy burden.
topics.trouble: Students apply Pike to discriminatory laws. Discriminatory laws face the near-per-se rule; Pike is for even-handed laws.

topics.title: The Market Participant Exception
topics.short: When a state acts as a buyer or seller rather than a regulator, it may prefer its own residents (Reeves, Inc. v. Stake, 1980); United Haulers (2007) also upheld laws favoring a public waste facility over private ones.
topics.trouble: Students think a state can use its spending to regulate anything downstream. The exception covers the state's own market dealings, not conditions it imposes on later private transactions (South-Central Timber, 1984).

topics.title: Privileges and Immunities of Article IV
topics.short: Article IV's Privileges and Immunities Clause bars states from discriminating against citizens of other states in fundamental matters such as earning a living, unless there is a substantial reason and a close relation to it (Toomer v. Witsell, 1948; Supreme Court of New Hampshire v. Piper, 1985).
topics.trouble: Students apply the clause to corporations. It protects citizens, which corporations are not for this purpose; the dormant commerce clause covers them.

topics.title: Youngstown and the Three Zones
topics.short: In Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952), 6 to 3, the Court held that President Truman lacked power to seize the steel mills; Justice Jackson's concurrence set out three zones: presidential power is greatest with Congress's authorization, uncertain in a "zone of twilight" when Congress is silent, and "at its lowest ebb" against Congress's will.
topics.trouble: Students quote Jackson's concurrence as the majority opinion. Justice Black wrote for the Court; Jackson's framework became the most cited part of the case.

topics.title: Nondelegation and Major Questions
topics.short: Congress may delegate authority to agencies if it lays down an "intelligible principle" (J. W. Hampton, 1928); the Court has struck down delegations to the government only twice (both in 1935); under the major questions doctrine (rooted in FDA v. Brown & Williamson, 2000) agencies need clear authorization for decisions of vast economic and political significance.
topics.trouble: Students think the nondelegation doctrine regularly strikes down laws. It has not been used to strike down a law since 1935, though several justices have called for reviving it (Gundy v. United States, 2019).

topics.title: Bicameralism, Presentment and the Line-Item Veto
topics.short: INS v. Chadha (1983) struck down the one-house legislative veto because lawmaking requires passage by both houses and presentment to the President; Clinton v. City of New York (1998) struck down the Line Item Veto Act for letting the President cancel parts of signed laws.
topics.trouble: Students think the line-item veto was struck down as too much power for Congress. It was struck down because canceling parts of a law amounts to amending it without following Article I's process.

topics.title: Appointments
topics.short: Principal officers are appointed by the President with Senate consent; Congress may vest the appointment of inferior officers in the President, courts or department heads (Edmond, 1997; Lucia v. SEC, 2018); recess appointments require a recess of at least ten days, presumptively (NLRB v. Noel Canning, 2014).
topics.trouble: Students think every executive employee is an "officer" needing Senate confirmation. Officers exercise significant authority under federal law; ordinary employees do not, and inferior officers may be appointed without the Senate if Congress so provides.

topics.title: The Removal Power
topics.short: Myers (1926) upheld the President's power to remove executive officers; Humphrey's Executor (1935) allowed limits for multi-member commissions; Morrison v. Olson (1988) upheld the independent counsel; and Seila Law (2020) struck down limits for a single agency director; the Court overruled Humphrey's Executor in 2026.
topics.trouble: Students think Humphrey's Executor protected every agency head. It covered only multi-member expert bodies, and Seila Law refused to extend it to a single director.

topics.title: Foreign Affairs
topics.short: United States v. Curtiss-Wright (1936) described broad presidential power in foreign affairs; Dames & Moore v. Regan (1981) upheld executive agreements settling the Iran hostage claims; Zivotofsky v. Kerry (2015) held the power to recognize foreign governments belongs to the President alone.
topics.trouble: Students think the President controls all foreign affairs. Congress regulates foreign commerce, declares war, funds the government and (through the Senate) approves treaties; Zivotofsky rested on the specific recognition power.

topics.title: War Powers and Detention
topics.short: The Prize Cases (1863) upheld Lincoln's blockade before Congress acted; after 2001, Hamdi v. Rumsfeld (2004) required due process for a citizen held as an enemy combatant, Hamdan v. Rumsfeld (2006) held military commissions unauthorized, and Boumediene v. Bush (2008) extended habeas corpus to detainees at Guantanamo Bay.
topics.trouble: Students think the Court gave the President a free hand in wartime. These cases mostly turned on whether Congress had authorized the action and on the Constitution's procedural protections.

topics.title: Executive Privilege and Presidential Immunity
topics.short: United States v. Nixon (1974) recognized a qualified executive privilege that yields to a criminal trial's need for evidence; Nixon v. Fitzgerald (1982) gave absolute civil immunity for official acts; and Clinton v. Jones (1997) allowed a civil suit about unofficial acts.
topics.trouble: Students mix up civil and criminal immunity, or official and unofficial acts. Sort each case by the kind of proceeding (civil or criminal) and the kind of act.

topics.title: Rational Basis Review
topics.short: Most laws get rational basis review: a law is upheld if it is rationally related to a legitimate government interest, and the challenger must negate every conceivable basis (Williamson v. Lee Optical, 1955); Carolene Products (1938) and its footnote four suggested closer review for some laws.
topics.trouble: Students think the government must prove its actual reason under rational basis. Any conceivable legitimate reason will do, and the burden is on the challenger.

topics.title: Intermediate and Strict Scrutiny
topics.short: Intermediate scrutiny requires an important government interest and means substantially related to it; strict scrutiny requires a compelling interest and means narrowly tailored (often, the least restrictive means), with the burden on the government.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the interest and the fit at each tier. Learn them as pairs: legitimate and rational; important and substantially related; compelling and narrowly tailored.

topics.title: Choosing the Tier
topics.short: The tier depends on what the law classifies or burdens: race, national origin and fundamental rights trigger strict scrutiny; sex and legitimacy intermediate; most economic and social laws rational basis; some areas use other tests instead, such as the Mathews balance for procedural due process.
topics.trouble: Students apply strict scrutiny to any law that seems unfair. First identify the classification or right; the tier follows from that, not from the law's wisdom.
